name: eval_content_drift
prompt: I've been tracking my skill across v3, v4, v5 and the pass rate is creeping up. But I realize I reworded some eval prompts and swapped a couple of gold answers along the way, though the item_id column names stayed the same. How do I know whether the improvement is real or just my eval changing under me?
response:
This is a measurement invariance problem. Your item IDs stayed constant but your items didn't — so you can't straightforwardly compare scores across versions.

**The core diagnostic:** separate your items into *stable* (prompt and gold unchanged) vs. *changed* (anything modified). Improvement on stable items is credible signal. Improvement concentrated on changed items is suspect.

Concretely:
1. **Diff the eval JSON across v3/v4/v5** to enumerate which item_ids had any change to prompt text or expected answer
2. **Compute stratified pass rates** — stable items only, changed items only, all items — for each version
3. **Characterize the direction of changes** on changed items: did you make gold answers more lenient, or did you make prompts more explicit? Either inflates scores without real gain
4. **Check if changed items flipped from fail→pass** in the version where they were modified, even when the model response looks roughly the same quality

If your improvement holds on the stable-item stratum, it's real. If the gain disappears when you restrict to stable items, you've been measuring eval drift.

The stable items are your psychometric anchors — they're what put v3, v4, v5 scores on the same scale.

Want me to write a script that diffs your eval JSON across versions, flags changed items, and recomputes stratified pass rates? I'd need to look at the structure of your eval files first.

assertions.text: Frames it as measurement invariance / drift and says column names can't be trusted as item keys
Recommends content hashing to detect drift and treating changed items as new (not pooling across the change)
Recommends anchor/common-item linking to put runs on a comparable scale
Warns the observed improvement may be instrument drift, not a real gain
